model.label: Three parallel subsectors: union-run and provincial social insurance funds (obras sociales) financed by payroll contributions, voluntary private prepaid plans, and a tax-funded public network (federal, provincial, municipal) open free to everyone; a mandatory minimum benefits basket (PMO) binds the first two

overview.statement: A 2026 review in Gaceta Sanitaria describes three subsectors: contributory social security (national, provincial, armed-forces and other obras sociales), which it says covers 38% of the population; private prepaid medicine, covering 5%; and a tax-funded public system to which every citizen has a right of free access.

The same review puts the share of people with social or private insurance at 43%, and says the other 57% of Argentines, of whom it states 27.5% are now poor, depend on public provision; it argues that only the insured could actually exercise market-style choice.

The health ministry's plain-language legal guide says obras sociales are insurance agents that must cover every benefit in the Programa Médico Obligatorio (PMO), plus the medicines those benefits require, and that all of them must be registered with the Superintendencia de Servicios de Salud.
Retirees are assigned to PAMI (the national institute for retirees and pensioners) when they retire, but may instead choose a registered obra social that accepts retirees.
Public hospitals may not refuse care to people who hold an obra social or prepaid plan, though the hospital may bill that insurer for the care it gave.

financing.statement: Employees pay 3% of salary to their obra social, plus 1.5% for each additional dependent beneficiary; the employer pays a further contribution as a percentage of pay (the government guide does not give the employer rate).
Self-employed workers in the monotributo simplified tax regime have their obra social contribution included in the monthly monotributo payment.

A Harvard-led 2020 report describes obras sociales as funded by compulsory payroll contributions of 3% of pay from employees and 6% from employers, with a Solidarity Redistribution Fund meant to offset differences between funds. It reports the employer rate as 6% while the plain-language legal guide gives no employer rate, so the rate should be checked against the law.
The report adds that only formally employed workers are covered by obras sociales, so coverage falls when unemployment or informal work rises.
The 2026 Gaceta Sanitaria review says total health spending is about 10% of GDP.
The review says Argentina is among the five Latin American countries spending the largest share of GDP on health, and also among the five where public money funds the smallest share.

Decree 102/2025 let prepaid medicine companies adjust the monthly fees of each plan freely for the whole life of a contract, with different percentages per plan, while still requiring notice to members at least 30 days before payment is due.

covered.statement: The PMO is a basic basket of benefits that every obra social and prepaid plan must cover at minimum under any of its plans, and no waiting period may be imposed for PMO benefits from the day of enrolment.
PMO maternal and child cover runs through the whole pregnancy and until one month after birth, then covers newborn care up to one year of age; hospital stays are covered in full.
PMO mental health cover is capped at 30 outpatient consultations a year (no more than 4 a month) and up to 30 days a year of inpatient care for acute conditions.
PMO rehabilitation covers physiotherapy and speech therapy up to 25 sessions a year.
PMO palliative care and outpatient dialysis are covered at 100%; palliative care applies when life expectancy is no more than six months.

A 2026 review says the PMO is currently enforceable only against social insurers and prepaid plans, not against the public sector, and that legislated coverage duties are placed on these insurers without a matching funding source; it says this widens inequity because the poorest people, covered only by the state, are not reached by them.

A Harvard-led 2020 report says the PMO, set up in 1995, has grown into one of the most inclusive benefit catalogues in the world, but its coding is badly outdated and there is no common nomenclature for diagnoses and procedures, so each payer or provider has built its own.

The same report says Argentina has no health technology assessment agency: the state mainly checks safety when new medicines and technologies are proposed for the benefit catalogue, and their clinical, social, ethical and economic implications are not evaluated.

cost_sharing.statement: Medicines in the PMO are generally covered at 40%; cover is 100% for cancer medicines, kidney failure medicines, medicines in special programmes and for hospital inpatients.
Permanent internal prostheses and implants are covered at 100% under the PMO, external orthoses and prostheses at 50%.
A doctor working for an obra social may charge the patient only the copayments (coseguros) set in the PMO.

financial_hardship.statement: In a cross-sectional study of frequent users of public health services in one interior Argentine city between March and October 2018, the odds of not obtaining medicines were 2.8 times higher when getting them required out-of-pocket spending; 80.51% of users who had to pay spent between USD 1 and 34.72. The sample is local and not nationally representative.

additional_care.statement: Prepaid medicine plans may not refuse cover for PMO practices, but may impose waiting periods for practices outside the PMO, which must be set out in the contract.
Formally employed workers may choose their obra social freely; during the switch procedure the previous obra social remains responsible for care for up to 3 months.

access.statement: A 2026 review says the Argentine system is one of the most accessible in the Americas, but that this access is not equal in quality or timeliness and its health results do not match its spending.
Physician supply is highly concentrated: the review's inequality table lists 1.66 doctors per 1,000 people in Buenos Aires city, against 0.18 in Misiones and 0.19 in Chaco.
Public spending per person differs widely by province: the review says Neuquén spends 6.2 times as much as Buenos Aires province, which is home to 40% of the population without health insurance.
According to the review, 5% of pregnant women receive no prenatal check, ranging from 0.1% in Tierra del Fuego to 8% in Misiones.

The review reports that women using the public sector reach their first breast cancer consultation at stage IV at double the share of women treated in the social security or private sectors, because of differences in diagnosis and treatment times.

A Harvard-led 2020 report says public hospitals have long had well-trained staff and good-quality services despite deteriorating infrastructure, scarce resources and long waits, and that insured people also use them for costly complex care for which hospitals are rarely reimbursed.

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2019 study, Argentina's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 59.9 (95% uncertainty interval 57.4-62.1) in 2019.

The review says the national infant mortality rate fell from 32.41 per 1,000 in 1980 to 8.5 in 2024, but the gap between best and worst provinces stayed at 2.8 times (4.9 in Buenos Aires city against 14 in Corrientes).
Maternal mortality is reported at 14.4 per 10,000 live births in Formosa against 2.3 in Buenos Aires city.
The review reports regional differences of 8 times in cervical cancer mortality and 3 times in colorectal cancer mortality.
The age-adjusted death rate is 5.3 per 1,000 in Buenos Aires city against 7.6 in Chaco.

costs.statement: According to CEPAL figures cited in the review, Argentina devotes a larger share of GDP to health than Uruguay, Chile and Costa Rica, yet those three countries achieve better results on life expectancy and infant mortality.
The review puts the national health authority's budget at less than half a point of GDP, and calls this a position of extreme weakness for balancing a federal system with deep income inequalities.

what_works.statement: The 2026 review says that during the pandemic the three subsectors almost spontaneously joined their service networks and offered enough capacity for demand, with excellent results.
Under the legal guide, obras sociales cannot require a medical exam before enrolment or reject people with disabilities, and PMO benefits carry no waiting period.

A 2024 commentary by authors including WHO economists says Programa Sumar, which started small and over 20 years grew by conditional transfers tied to results in a highly decentralised system, shows that strengthening one scheme need not mean fragmentation.
The Harvard-led report notes that reforming the Solidarity Redistribution Fund and introducing a single basic package for the insured was an important step toward equity and transparency.

verification.note: Statement copies 12+ consecutive words from the source; rewrite in own words.

problems.statement: The review concludes that the system has no policy defining the financing and care model, and that in more than 40 years of democracy Argentina has not decided what role the state plays in health.

The Harvard-led report says historical decentralisation without a plan to unify the sector left no coordination mechanisms across systems and subnational bodies, causing inefficient use of resources and highly unequal access to quality services.
The same report says no formal clearing or reimbursement mechanism exists between coverage segments, so an insured person may be treated free in a public facility and the insurer never billed.

The report cites an estimate that 30 to 50% of the population has double or triple affiliation, for example both an obra social and private cover or PAMI, which makes dependence on each subsector hard to measure.

The review states that the 1990s free choice of obra social led to 'creaming' of higher-income members towards prepaid companies, which it says were probably the only winners, and that public finances did not improve with hospital self-management.

reforms.statement: The Superintendency presents decree 102/2025 as a further step in the deregulation begun by emergency decree DNU 70/23, aimed at free competition and members' freedom of choice.

The 2026 review says the Milei government substantially cut the federal health budget and transfers to provinces, arguing health is a provincial responsibility, and that its health measures aim almost entirely at market deregulation and citizen choice.
The review's author says it is too early for a full evaluation of current policy and that effects on access, outcomes and sustainability can only be measured in coming years.

The review lists earlier failed integration attempts: Ramón Carrillo's 1940s plan to merge obra social resources into one public system, the Sistema Nacional Integrado de Salud, and the Seguro Nacional de Salud under Alfonsín, each undone by conflict with union-run obras sociales.
